title: Distinguish drawing priority from no preference in Canvas 2D

labels.name: needs implementer interest
labels.description: Moving the issue forward requires implementers to express interest

body:
### What problem are you trying to solve?

A Canvas 2D application may draw frequently and also perform repeated pixel readbacks. If an optimization makes readbacks faster at the cost of slower drawing, the application may prefer to accept the readback cost. Readback frequency alone does not tell the user agent which trade-off the author wants.

The [HTML Standard](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/canvas.html#canvasrenderingcontext2dsettings) defines `willReadFrequently` as a boolean that defaults to `false`. Setting it to `true` signals frequent readbacks and allows the user agent to optimize for them. Both omission and `false` leave the user agent free to choose its optimizations; neither expresses a preference for drawing performance over readback performance.

An explicit drawing preference would let authors communicate that choice while keeping automatic decisions available to applications with no preference.

### What solutions exist today?

Authors can rely on the user agent to choose a suitable rendering strategy. It may already choose the strategy the application prefers, but the current standard provides no way to communicate drawing priority when the two disagree.

Blink distinguishes an omitted `willReadFrequently` value from an explicit `false`: omission permits its readback-triggered fallback from GPU to CPU rendering, while explicit `false` skips that fallback. Authors can use this distinction in Blink, but it has no standardized meaning. The behavior is discussed in [this Chromium review](https://chromium-review.googlesource.com/c/chromium/src/+/8173003).

### How would you solve it?

Allow authors to express three preferences when creating a 2D context:

- Prefer readback performance.
- Prefer drawing performance, accepting higher readback costs when the two conflict.
- Leave the choice to the user agent.

These would be optimization hints. The user agent would retain control over the rendering implementation and could account for device constraints. A preference would carry no guarantee of GPU rendering or a particular performance result.

The API representation is open. A separate preference member could preserve the existing meaning of `willReadFrequently`. Its interaction with the boolean would need to be defined. Giving explicit `false` a new drawing-priority meaning would require compatibility evidence, since applications and libraries may already pass it as a default without intending that preference. Input conversions would also need review if the member's type changed.

The requested preference should also survive settings reuse. A library may receive a context and create another for the same rendering role:

```javascript
function createReplacementContext(original) {
  const canvas = document.createElement("canvas");
  canvas.width = original.canvas.width;
  canvas.height = original.canvas.height;
  return canvas.getContext("2d", original.getContextAttributes());
}
```

Today, `getContextAttributes()` returns `willReadFrequently: false` for both omission and explicit `false`, so this code loses Blink's distinction. Applications can retain their original options separately, but a library that receives only a context cannot recover them through this method.

If the standard exposes separate preferences, `getContextAttributes()` should report the requested preference, including no preference, so the code above preserves it. That value should describe the author's request independently of the context's current CPU or GPU backing. Changes to the returned settings would also need compatibility review.

### Anything else?

The original `willReadFrequently` proposal is in [whatwg/html#5614](https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/5614). [Priority Hints](https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/7150) and [WebGL's power-preference work](https://github.com/KhronosGroup/WebGL/issues/2282) provide API design precedents for distinguishing opposing preferences from an automatic choice.

Would other implementers find a drawing preference useful for workloads that combine drawing and readbacks? Examples where automatic decisions conflict with the application's preferred trade-off, along with drawing and readback measurements, would help assess the benefit.
